source_category: Public-opinion poll (context only; not outcome evidence)
locator: Report sections “Key Takeaways,” “Voters Favor Strong Public Oversight of EdTech and AI,” and methodology note 48
limitations: Opinion context only; excluded from evidence register and participant totals.

finding: New York Senate Bill S10685 (FOCUS Act) §§ 31, 33 and 37(2) Operative Text
design: Proposed state legislation; educational policy crosswalk, not legal advice or empirical evidence.
value: § 31(1) p. 3 (PK–5 school-issued device ban and on-campus electronic/internet-enabled device restriction) | § 33(1)(a)–(g) pp. 4–5 (bars social media, gaming, messaging, AI companions, generative AI, conversational AI preserving disability assistive tech, and cameras) | § 37(2) p. 7 (“inherent to the learning objective of an activity, assignment, assessment or task”)
evidence_units: Proposed NY Senate Bill S10685 (introduced Aug. 21, 2026)
sample_scope: Proposed New York State public school statutory framework
source_category: Proposed state legislation (educational analysis, not legal advice)
locator: Official bill PDF: § 31(1) p. 3; § 33(1)–(2) pp. 4–5; § 37(2)–(3) p. 7 (also at https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/bills/2025/S10685)
limitations: Neutral, product-free educational questions added to crosswalk; explicitly labeled not legal advice. Exact § 37(2) wording includes four nouns (“activity, assignment, assessment or task”).

finding: Early-years interactive math apps: supplemental vs control
design: Pupil-level randomized controlled trial
sample_scope: 126 supplemental vs 132 control (389 posttested across all 3 arms; 461 randomized); overlaps M4 and D1/D2
locator: Journal of Educational Psychology 111(2), pp. 284-297 (packet printed 284-298); Results p. 291 (t(256) = 2.46, p = 0.015); DOI https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000286
limitations: Supplemental arm added 30 minutes daily of math app instruction atop regular classroom math. Shares 132-pupil control with M4 and is included in Dorris et al. (2024) D1/D2; never sum participant totals across rows.

finding: Early-years interactive math apps: time-equivalent replacement vs control
design: Pupil-level randomized controlled trial
sample_scope: 131 time-equivalent replacement vs 132 control; shares control with M3 and overlaps D1/D2
locator: Results p. 291 (t(261) = 1.74, directional one-tailed p = 0.042; Group 1 vs Group 2 d = 0.08 [-0.17, 0.33], p = 0.525)
limitations: Authors report significance under a directional one-tailed test (p = 0.042), while the printed two-tailed 95% CI [-0.03, 0.46] crosses zero. Shares 132-pupil control with M3 and overlaps D1/D2.

finding: Intelligent tutoring systems: overall learning outcomes
design: Random-effects meta-analysis of experimental and quasi-experimental evaluations
sample_scope: Elementary through postsecondary (60 of 107 effects postsecondary, N = 6,767; K-5 k = 19, N = 1,496, g = 0.31 [0.16, 0.47])
locator: Table 1 p. 907 (overall random-effects g = 0.41 [0.34, 0.48], I-squared = 73%; large-group g = 0.44 [0.35, 0.53], non-ITS CBI g = 0.57 [0.34, 0.79], textbooks/workbooks g = 0.36 [0.18, 0.53], small-group g = 0.05 [-0.50, 0.61]); Table 3 p. 909; DOI https://doi.org/10.1037/a0037123
limitations: Pre-LLM systems and majority postsecondary sample. Abstract p. 901 prints .42 and .35 for two comparators where p. 906 and Table 1 p. 907 report random-effects 0.44 and 0.36. Overlaps Kulik & Fletcher (2016) and Steenbergen-Hu & Cooper (2013); never sum samples.

finding: Intelligent tutoring systems vs individual human tutoring
design: Random-effects comparator subgroup in meta-analysis
sample_scope: Comparator subgroup within M5 (do not add 404 to 14,321)
locator: Table 1 p. 907 (Comparison treatment: Individual human tutoring, k = 5, N = 404, random-effects g = -0.11 [-0.31, 0.10]; small-group human instruction k = 4, N = 184, g = 0.05 [-0.50, 0.61])
limitations: Null difference against one-to-one human tutoring (point estimate slightly favors human tutoring, 95% CI crosses zero). Included alongside M5 to preserve comparator symmetry.

finding: Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning: Evidence from high school mathematics
design: Preregistered three-arm classroom-cluster randomized controlled trial
metric: Normalized 0-to-1 exam and practice regression coefficients (classroom-clustered SEs)
value: Practice: GPT Base +0.137 (SE 0.031, +48%), GPT Tutor +0.361 (SE 0.032, +127%) vs 0.284 control | Unaided exam: GPT Base -0.054 (SE 0.022, p < 0.05, -17%), GPT Tutor -0.004 (SE 0.013, null) vs 0.321 control | GPT Base accuracy 51% (42% logical, 8% arithmetic errors); 67% vs 37% superficial first queries
sample_scope: Nearly 1,000 high-school math students (grades 9-11) in Turkey, fall 2023
locator: PNAS 122(26), e2422633122 (DOI https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2422633122): Abstract; Experimental Design; Table 1 (2,848 observations); Potential Mechanism (51% accuracy, 67% vs 37% superficial); Aug. 20, 2025 affiliation correction https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2518204122
limitations: Narrative card only: regression outcomes are normalized 0-to-1 scores with SEs rather than reported d/g and 95% CIs. Four-session high-school math study, not elementary or reading evidence.

finding: AI tutoring outperforms in-class active learning: Harvard undergraduate physics crossover RCT
design: Two-lesson peer-group-randomized crossover trial
metric: Post-test medians (0-5 scale) and OLS/quantile regression SD estimates (95% CIs NR)
value: Median post-test 4.5 (N = 142) vs 3.5 (N = 174) from 2.75 baseline (N = 316), z = -5.6, p < 10^-8 | Median time 49 min (70% < 60 min) vs 60 min class | OLS 0.63 SD; quantile 0.73 to 1.3 SD | Engagement 4.1 vs 3.6; motivation 3.4 vs 3.1
sample_scope: HIGHER EDUCATION (Harvard University Physical Sciences 2 undergraduates, fall 2023); not K-12
locator: Scientific Reports 15, 17458 (DOI https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-97652-6): Results (Learning gains, Time on task, Linear regression, Perceptions); Methods (233 enrolled, 194 eligible, IRB23-0797)
limitations: Narrative card only: 95% CIs NR in main text and sample is Harvard undergraduates across two immediate-posttest physics lessons with no delayed retention test.

finding: One Click Away: AI Tutoring with Khanmigo in a Two-Year School Experiment
design: Preregistered (AEARCTR-0013519) two-year grade-within-school cluster randomized trial
metric: MAP math NPR, RIT and population/control SD regressions with cluster-robust SEs
value: Pooled term (6,902 student-terms, 53 clusters): +1.264 NPR (SE 0.597; +1.216 full controls), +0.758 RIT (SE 0.379), +0.040 pop. SD/term (SE 0.019) | Annual (2,759 student-years): Year 1 +0.020 pop. SD (SE 0.035, null), Year 2 +0.084 pop. SD (SE 0.041, p < 0.05; +0.116 RTI control SD, SE 0.053; implied participant +0.142), stacked +0.062 pop. SD (SE 0.035) | Chatbot use: 96% tried once, median 1/3 practice days, 17% of mistake sessions, 14.5% math reasoning/questions; ~$15/student/yr
evidence_units: 18 middle schools; 53 grade-within-school clusters; 6,902 student-terms; 2,759 student-years
sample_scope: Hamilton County, Tennessee public middle schools in remedial RTI math (2024-25 and 2025-26)
locator: NBER Working Paper 35620 (Aug. 2026, https://www.nber.org/papers/w35620): Abstract & pp. 3-4; Table 3 p. 17; Table 5 p. 22; Table 7 p. 24
limitations: Narrative card only: non-peer-reviewed working paper reporting SEs rather than printed 95% CIs. Bundled Khan Academy practice with Khanmigo; sparse chatbot dialogue means gains cannot be attributed to AI conversation over structured practice.

finding: Tutor CoPilot: A Human-AI Approach for Scaling Real-Time Expertise
design: Preregistered (osf.io/8d6ha) seven-week tutor-level randomized controlled trial
metric: Session exit-ticket mastery percentage-point ITT (clustered SEs and Romano-Wolf p-values)
value: Unconditional exit-ticket pass +4 pp (+0.040, SE 0.015, RW p = 0.010, ~61.7% to 65.7% across 4,136 sessions); conditional +3.1 pp (+0.031, SE 0.014, RW p = 0.040) | Lower-rated tutors +9 pp (56% to 65%); less-experienced tutors +7 pp (61% to 68%) | ~$20/tutor/yr API cost; non-experimental EOY MAP projection 0.024 SD
evidence_units: 783 active tutors (388 T, 395 C of 900 randomized); 1,013 students; 4,136 sessions
sample_scope: Below-grade-level students in grades 3-6 across 9 Title I schools in a southern U.S. district (virtual FEV Tutor math sessions, spring 2024)
locator: EdWorkingPaper 24-1056 (Nov. 2025, DOI https://doi.org/10.26300/81nh-8262; PDF header prints 24-1054_v2): Abstract, pp. 2-5, Table 1 pp. 4 & 16, Fig. 2 p. 5, Methods p. 12, Competing Interests p. 17
limitations: Narrative card only: working paper measuring tutor-facing AI on immediate session exit tickets (not student-facing chatbots or direct EOY MAP achievement). First author worked part-time with FEV Tutor to integrate the tool; earlier Oct. 2024 arXiv 2410.03017 reported randomized pool (900 tutors / ~1,800 students).

finding: WITHHELD UNDER SOURCE GOVERNANCE: Computer-assisted learning in the real world: How Khan Academy influences student math learning
design: Three-year within-teacher and within-school longitudinal administrative panel (observational/quasi-experimental; not randomized)
metric: Withheld from register and narrative cards under vendor-efficacy exclusion rule
value: Verified values documented in audit only: 203,465 unique grades 3-8 students across 213,907 student-year observations (packet printed 'about 214,000 students'); +0.031 SD at 6.6 annual hours (~11 min/wk) and projected +0.085 SD at 30 min/wk; 10% met recommended usage and 24% logged zero usage
sample_scope: U.S. districts licensing Khan Academy MAP Accelerator in grades 3-8
locator: PNAS 123(1), e2507708123 (DOI https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2507708123) and March 4, 2026 PNAS Correction 123(10), e2604984123 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12974481/)
limitations: Excluded from both the numerical register and narrative study cards under standing source-governance rules barring vendor-produced or vendor-coauthored product efficacy research: coauthors Bogdan Yamkovenko and Kodi Weatherholtz are Khan Academy Efficacy Research employees holding the proprietary dataset, and the March 4, 2026 PNAS Correction discloses that Emma Brunskill and Philip Oreopoulos served on Khan Academy's informal research advisory committee (2021-2024, uncompensated).

finding: Phone-Free Schools and Achievement Growth: A Student-Level Analysis (lockable Yondr pouches and 2025-26 state phone bans)
design: Doubly robust staggered difference-in-differences and quantile regression with propensity weighting on student-level NWEA MAP Growth and mobile geolocation pings
metric: Annual student achievement growth in SD units (school-clustered SEs; 95% CIs NR in main tables)
value: Yondr pouches: phone pings -11% Year 1, -20% Year 2+ | Pooled growth +0.0087 SD (SE 0.0043, p < 0.05), math +0.0079 SD (SE 0.0049), reading +0.0095 SD (SE 0.0052) (~1-2 weeks/yr) | Reading Q10 +0.0172 SD (SE 0.0066) vs Q90 +0.0022 SD (SE 0.0049) | Non-causal 2025-26 state bans: +0.015 SD reading (bell-to-bell), +0.019 SD math (instructional-time)
evidence_units: 4,600 schools (Table 1 math: 677 Yondr vs 3,347 comparison schools); 9,941,182 pooled student-year observations (4,688,902 math, 5,252,280 reading)
sample_scope: U.S. Grades 3-10 public and charter school students across 49 states and D.C., 2021-22 through 2025-26
locator: Harvard CEPR report (Nov. 17, 2026, https://cepr.harvard.edu/resource/phone-free-schools-report): p. 1 funding; p. 2 Abstract; pp. 4-5 state bans; p. 18 Table 1; p. 19 Fig. 5; p. 21 Table 2; p. 26 Table 3; pp. 27-32 Tables 4-5
limitations: Narrative card only: non-peer-reviewed report funded by Overdeck and Walton Family Foundations (Yondr supplied school purchase records); main tables report school-clustered SEs rather than 95% CIs; authors warn 2025-26 state-ban estimates are non-causal due to pre-trends and 2020-21 in-person schooling imbalance (71.44% vs 21.15% unweighted / 60.06% weighted); tests personal smartphones, not classroom computers.

finding: Technology and Child Development: Evidence from the One Laptop per Child Program (rural Peru RCT)
design: School-level cluster randomized controlled trial over 15 months
metric: Computers-per-student ratio and standardized math/language/cognitive scores (2017 journal table CIs NR behind AEA paywall; 2012 IDB working paper reports SEs)
value: 2017 AEJ abstract: computers/student 0.12 to 1.18 across 318 schools, substantial school/home use gains, null math/language effects, inconclusive cognitive effects | 2012 IDB-WP-304: school use 26% to 82%, home use 4% to 42%, average Math/Language +0.003 SD (SE 0.055, null), cognitive composite +0.11 SD (p = 0.068)
evidence_units: 318 rural primary schools in published 2017 article (319 schools: 209 T, 110 C in 2012 IDB-WP-304)
sample_scope: Rural public primary schools in Peru after 15 months of One Laptop per Child implementation
locator: AEJ: Applied Economics 9(3), 295-320 (DOI https://doi.org/10.1257/app.20150385) p. 295 official abstract; open-access 2012 IDB Working Paper IDB-WP-304 pp. 1-4, 7-8 (https://publications.iadb.org/publications/english/document/Technology-and-Child-Development-Evidence-from-the-One-Laptop-per-Child-Program.pdf)
limitations: Narrative card only: full 2017 journal regression tables are paywalled (95% CIs NR in public AEA record) and open-access 2012 working paper reports SEs rather than 95% CIs. Schools lacked internet connectivity, curriculum-aligned math/language software, and pedagogical integration.

finding: Global Education Monitoring Report 2023: Technology in Education: A Tool on Whose Terms?
design: Intergovernmental global monitoring synthesis of cross-national assessments, systematic reviews and country evaluations
metric: Descriptive cross-national shares and qualitative synthesis (no pooled meta-analytic effect size)
value: PISA 2018 ~10% of 15-year-olds across 50+ systems used classroom devices >1 hr/wk in math/science | >1 in 3 teachers across 7 ICILS 2018 countries agreed classroom ICT caused distraction | 31% (500M+) students unreached by COVID-19 remote learning (72% poorest) | 1 in 4 primary schools lacked electricity (2021) | UK interactive whiteboards largely replaced blackboards; Peru >1M OLPC laptops yielded no learning gain
evidence_units: Global synthesis (PISA 2018 50+ systems; ICILS 2018 12 systems; global policy/infrastructure inventories)
sample_scope: Global education systems (pre-primary through higher education)
locator: UNESCO 2023 GEM Report (DOI 10.54676/UZQV8501, https://gem-report-2023.unesco.org/technology-in-education/): Ch. 1 Introduction, Ch. 2 Equity, Ch. 4 Teaching and Learning, Ch. 7 Access
limitations: Narrative card only: intergovernmental synthesis report with no pooled effect size or 95% CI. Descriptive PISA/ICILS shares are observational and predate generative AI.

finding: The effectiveness of educational technology applications for enhancing mathematics achievement in K-12 classrooms: A meta-analysis
design: Random-effects and mixed-effects meta-analysis of controlled experimental and matched quasi-experimental evaluations (12+ weeks duration)
metric: Unlabeled covariate-adjusted standardized effect size ES (Section 6.4 p. 95 does not confirm Cohen d vs Hedges g)
evidence_units: 74 K-12 math studies (45 elementary, 29 secondary; 26 randomized, 48 quasi-experimental)
sample_scope: K-12 mathematics classrooms (Grades 1-12; elementary N = 31,555, secondary N = 25,331; 1980s-2011)
locator: Educational Research Review 9, 88-113 (ERIC EJ999451): Abstract p. 88; Sec. 6.4 p. 95; Tables 2-4 p. 96; Sec. 7.2.3 & Table 9 p. 98; Conclusion p. 102
limitations: Narrative card only: Section 6.4 prints unlabeled ES without confirming Cohen d vs Hedges g, and 1980s-2011 K-12 math studies substantially overlap Ran, Kim & Secada (2022) in M1 and Steenbergen-Hu & Cooper (2013) (never sum participant counts). External funding sponsor NR in accessed article text.

finding: WITHHELD SECONDARY COMMENTARY: The Problem With Ed Tech Isn’t Screen Time (Hari Subramonyam, Nov. 20, 2026 Substack essay)
design: Opinion/commentary essay citing external studies
metric: Excluded from register and narrative cards as opinion commentary
value: NR
sample_scope: Opinion commentary (non-empirical)
locator: Published Nov. 20, 2026 on Substack; outbound empirical/official citations extracted and audited against original publications
limitations: Excluded under source governance because commentary essays are not outcome evidence; its four new underlying primary/intergovernmental sources (Harvard CEPR 2026, Cristia et al. 2017, UNESCO 2023, Cheung & Slavin 2013) were verified and added directly.
